Name: A seed company had this corn farmer PROSECUTED for breeding his own seed, and Indonesia's highest court later gutted the law they used
Copy:
Tukirin, a corn grower in the Nganjuk district of East Java, was convicted in 2005 after a seed company accused him of breeding and planting corn seed he had developed himself

He received a suspended prison sentence and an order not to plant his own seed for a year, under a law reserving seed certification for the government and licensed bodies

More than a dozen growers in Nganjuk and Kediri were prosecuted between 2005 and 2010 before Indonesia's Constitutional Court found key parts of that law unconstitutional
CTA:
Support farmers who save their own seed

Find them on Localize
context: Tukirin, a corn farmer in Nganjuk regency, East Java, was prosecuted in 2005 after a seed company accused him of breeding his own corn seed; he got a suspended sentence and was barred from planting his own seed for a year under Article 14(1) of Indonesia's plant cultivation law, which reserves seed certification to the government and authorised bodies. More than a dozen farmers in Nganjuk and Kediri regencies were prosecuted between 2005 and 2010. A judicial review at Indonesia's Constitutional Court subsequently found key articles unconstitutional (reported 2013). Sources: GRAIN, 'Indonesian farmers prosecuted for breeding their own seeds'; Asian Farmers Association case documentation; Resilience.org, 'Our seed, our sovereignty - seed law victory in Indonesia' (2013); Critical Asian Studies 52(4), 'Farmer-plant-breeders and the law on Java, Indonesia'. LEFT OUT: Tukirin's age is given as 53 in one account only, so it is not in the Copy. DEDUPE: checked %indonesia%, %seed law%, %tukirin%, %nganjuk% against Master; the only Indonesia rows are tofu factories, rainforest clearing for sugarcane and seaweed packaging. Fresh angle.

Name: A city whose motto is WHERE EVERYTHING GROWS fined a man 750 dollars for growing food in his own front yard
Copy:
Michael Sherman tore out his front lawn in Chino, California in 2019 and replaced it with a food forest of passionfruit, radishes, sunflowers, Swiss chard and bananas

After neighbors complained the city issued 750 dollars in code fines and told him to clear overgrowth and keep crops 15 feet back from the yards next door

His next door neighbors are not the ones complaining, and say he is constantly offering them food and checking whether the garden has gotten to be too much
CTA:
Support home growers and food freedom

Find yours on Localize
context: Michael Sherman replaced his Chino, California front lawn with a 'food forest' in 2019, growing passionfruit, radishes, calendulas, sunflowers, aloe vera, Swiss chard and bananas. After repeated neighbor complaints the city issued $750 in fines for code violations and required him to remove overgrown vegetation, maintain a line of sight, and keep crops from growing within 15 feet of neighboring yards. Chino's city motto is 'Where everything grows.' Supportive next-door neighbors are quoted saying he regularly offers them food. Sources: CBS Los Angeles, 'Chino man's home garden sparks debate amongst neighbors'; Champion Newspapers, 'Chino resident fights for freedom to grow food garden' (2026). LEFT OUT: some aggregator write-ups frame this as an HOA fine; CBS LA reports it as city code enforcement, so the Copy says city. DEDUPE: checked %chino%, %front yard%, %vegetable garden%; existing rows cover Miami Shores FL, Oak Park MI, Tulsa OK and a Florida couple's six-year fight, all different places and mechanisms. Fresh angle. Worth a human check: this is live 2026 enforcement and the fine could be resolved or appealed before posting.

Name: A county sued a farmer for growing TOO MANY vegetables, then kept prosecuting him after he fixed the zoning
Copy:
Steve Miller had spent about 15 years growing figs, broccoli and cabbage on two acres in Clarkston, Georgia, selling at farmers markets and giving much of the harvest away

DeKalb County code officers began ticketing him in 2010 for growing more crops than his zoning allowed, and the county sued him for 5,000 dollars in fines

He stopped planting and had the land rezoned, and about two weeks after approval the county revived the old charges because he had been in violation before the change
CTA:
Support growers feeding their own towns

See them near you with Localize
context: Steve Miller grew figs, broccoli and cabbages on just over two acres in Clarkston, DeKalb County, Georgia, after roughly 15 years of growing to sell at farmers markets and give away. DeKalb County code enforcement began ticketing him in January 2010 for growing too many crops for his zoning and for unpermitted workers on site; the county sued for $5,000 in fines. Neighbors dubbed it 'Cabbagegate.' He stopped growing and got the property rezoned, then about two weeks after approval the county resumed prosecuting the earlier charges on the grounds that he had been in violation before the rezoning. Sources: Atlanta Journal-Constitution, 'County cites farmer for too many vegetables'; WSB-TV Atlanta, 'County Sues Farmer, Cites Too Many Crops'; Atlanta Magazine, 'A guy, a garden and an anti-veggie zoning code'; Grist; UPI. DEDUPE: checked %clarkston%, %dekalb%, %too many%, %georgia%; no existing row covers this case. Fresh angle.

Name: A seed company sued a nonprofit for selling old vegetable seeds, and Europe's highest court sided with the seed company
Copy:
Kokopelli is a French association that sells thousands of old vegetable varieties, most of them not entered on the official European catalogue of approved seed

Selling a variety that is not on that list is unlawful, and the commercial seed firm Graines Baumaux took Kokopelli to court over exactly that

The European Court of Justice ruled on 12 July 2012 that the restriction was justified, leaving the catalogue rules standing across the bloc
CTA:
Support seed savers keeping old varieties alive

The ones near you are on Localize
context: Association Kokopelli, a French seed-saving nonprofit, sells thousands of traditional and rare vegetable varieties, most not listed on the official EU common catalogue of vegetable varieties; marketing an uncatalogued variety is unlawful under EU seed marketing directives. Commercial seed company Graines Baumaux brought proceedings against Kokopelli in 2007 for unfair competition on that basis. The Court of Justice of the European Union decided Case C-59/11, Association Kokopelli v Graines Baumaux SAS, on 12 July 2012, holding the restriction on the freedom to pursue an economic activity justified and upholding the directives. Sources: German Law Journal (Cambridge Core), 'Fundamental Freedoms, Fundamental Rights, and the Scope of Free Movement Law', which summarizes the C-59/11 holding and date; Corporate Europe Observatory, 'Closing in on our seeds'; organic-market.info. LEFT OUT: the fine imposed on Kokopelli by the French courts is reported inconsistently across secondary sources (10,000 euros in one account, 35,000 euros in others), so no figure appears in the Copy. Note: curia.europa.eu and eur-lex.europa.eu were both blocked by the network proxy on this run, so the primary judgment text was not read directly. Worth a human check before scripting. DEDUPE: checked %kokopelli%, %france%, %heirloom seed%, %catalogue%, %europe%; the one adjacent row is 'Some heirloom seeds are now illegal to save and replant because they got patented', a patent story rather than the EU catalogue mechanism. Fresh angle.

Name: Japan repealed the law guaranteeing public seed for rice and wheat, so its own prefectures started writing it back in one by one
Copy:
The Main Crop Seeds Act of 1952 required all 47 Japanese prefectures to maintain and supply quality public seed for rice, wheat, barley and soybeans

Japan repealed it on 1 April 2018, ending that national obligation and opening staple seed development further to private companies

Prefectures answered by passing seed ordinances of their own, Niigata, Hyogo and Saitama among the first, to keep staple seed development in public hands
CTA:
Support farmers growing from public seed

Find the closest ones on Localize
context: Japan's Main Crop Seeds Law (Shubyo Ho), enacted 1952, obliged each of the 47 prefectures to maintain and supply good quality seed of staple crops: rice, wheat, barley and soybeans. It was repealed effective 1 April 2018. Prefectures responded by enacting their own local seed ordinances (shushi jorei) to preserve public involvement in staple seed development, production and quality control; Niigata, Hyogo and Saitama were among the first, with Nagano, Toyama, Hokkaido and Yamagata following. Sources: The Japan Times, 'Abolition of Main Crop Seeds Law puts nation at risk' (20 March 2018); GRAIN, 'Saving Japan's seed heritage from free trade'; Local Futures / Resilience.org. LEFT OUT: one lower-quality secondary source claims more than 30 prefectures had passed ordinances by early 2024; that figure could not be confirmed against a reliable source and is not in the Copy. DEDUPE: checked %japan%, %prefect%, %seed law%; existing Japan rows cover school lunches, red netting, CSA boxes, rooftop gardens and honor-box stands. Fresh angle.

Name: An English city gave residents the right to grow food on council land and became the first in the country to do it
Copy:
Hull councillors passed a Right to Grow motion in September 2023, the first UK city to adopt one, committing the council to map the unused land it owns

The scheme licenses community groups to plant food, fruit bushes and wildflowers on those council plots, with applications answered inside 15 working days

The council also helps growers past the practical things that usually kill these projects, like insurance and getting water out to the plot
CTA:
Support community growers

Find them in your area on Localize
context: Hull City Council unanimously passed a 'Right to Grow' motion in September 2023, the first UK city to do so, committing the council to produce a map of suitable council-owned land and to help would-be growers with practical obstacles such as insurance and water provision. In 2025 Hull launched the scheme itself, making council-owned land available for cultivation by community organisations under a simple licence covering food, plants, wildflowers and fruit bushes; applications are reviewed and answered within 15 working days. Sources: Hull City Council, 'Right to grow' scheme pages and 19 May 2025 announcement; Sustain, 'Hull residents given new Right to Grow Food in historic council motion' (Oct 2023); Sustainable Food Places; Incredible Edible. DEDUPE: checked %hull%, %right to grow%, %england%; existing rows cover Todmorden's public planting and a US-versus-UK HOA comparison, neither of which is this council-land mechanism. Fresh angle.

Name: For 85 years Congress mailed Americans free seed by the tens of millions of packets, until the seed industry got it killed
Copy:
Congressional seed distribution began in 1839 and grew into a program where members of Congress sent free seed packets to constituents through the Agriculture Department

In fiscal year 1902 alone Congress put 270,000 dollars behind it and members sent out more than 37 million packets of vegetable seed and another million of flower seed

The American Seed Trade Association, formed by private seed companies, spent decades lobbying against the program and Congress ended it in 1924
CTA:
Support seed savers and small growers

See who is near you on Localize
context: Congressional seed distribution ran from 1839 to 1924: members of Congress directed the free distribution of seed packets to farmers and constituents through the US Department of Agriculture. In fiscal year 1902 Congress appropriated $270,000 and members distributed 37,299,816 packets of vegetable seed and 1,000,568 packets of flower seed. The American Seed Trade Association, formed in the late 1800s by private seed companies, made ending the free seed program one of its primary lobbying goals; Congress ended it in 1924. Sources: US House of Representatives History, Art & Archives, 'Seed Distribution, Department of Agriculture' and the 'Gone to Seed' blog entry; Journal of the Gilded Age and Progressive Era (Cambridge), 'Who Wants White Carrots? Congressional Seed Distribution, 1862 to 1923'; Atlas Obscura. NOTE: sources vary between 1923 and 1924 for the final year, with most citing 1924; the headline's '85 years' counts 1839 to 1924. DEDUPE: checked %free seed%, %seed packet%, %congress%seed%, %mailed%, %victory garden%; the existing Victory Gardens row is a different program and era. Fresh angle.

Name: Argentina's economy collapsed and a quarter of this city lost its job, so the city handed out land instead of handouts
Copy:
When Argentina's economy collapsed in 2001, roughly a quarter of Rosario's workforce lost their jobs and more than half the city's population fell below the poverty line

The city's Urban Agriculture Program set out to work with 20 groups of growers and had grown to around 800 urban farming projects by 2004

Produce from those gardens went to feeding about 40,000 residents, and close to 300 growers now hold temporary rights to public and private land, most of them women
CTA:
Support urban growers feeding their cities

Look for them near you on Localize
context: Argentina's 2001 economic collapse left about a quarter of Rosario's workforce unemployed and more than half its population below the poverty line. The municipality, with local and national NGOs, launched the Urban Agriculture Program (UAP), providing land access, equipment, training and seed. It planned to work with 20 farmer groups and had expanded to roughly 800 urban farming projects by 2004. Produce from the gardens helped meet the nutrition needs of about 40,000 residents; today close to 300 urban farmers hold temporary tenure over public and private land, about 65% of them women, selling at Rosario's markets. Sources: World Resources Institute, 'Rosario, Argentina Uses Urban Farming to Tackle Economic and Climate Crises'; World Economic Forum (2021); ICLEI Circulars case study; IDRC case study; Mongabay (Dec 2021). LEFT OUT: the WRI Ross Center Prize for Cities recognition is described inconsistently across sources as finalist versus winner for the 2020-2021 cycle, and prizeforcities.org was blocked by the network proxy on this run, so no prize claim appears in the Copy. DEDUPE: checked %rosario%, %argentina%, %urban agriculture%; existing Argentina rows are all beef imports and recalls, and the urban-farming rows cover Havana, Detroit, Atlanta, Houston and Singapore. Fresh angle.

Name: Australia has the largest wild camel herd on Earth and sent snipers in helicopters to shoot 5,000 of them in five days
Copy:
Camels brought to Australia in the 1800s went feral and now roam the outback in the largest wild camel population anywhere, running into the hundreds of thousands

In January 2020 marksmen in helicopters killed more than 5,000 of them over five days in the APY Lands of South Australia, the first cull of its kind in that state

Drought had pushed the herds into remote communities of around 2,300 people, where they drained scarce water, damaged infrastructure and became a hazard on the roads
CTA:
Support producers raising real meat

Find them close to home on Localize
context: Camels imported to Australia in the 1800s established the world's largest feral camel population, estimated from several hundred thousand up to about a million. In January 2020, helicopter-borne marksmen killed more than 5,000 feral camels over a five-day cull in the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands of north-west South Australia, home to about 2,300 Indigenous people; the target was up to 10,000 and it was the first cull of its kind in that state. Officials cited extremely large herds encroaching on communities, threatening scarce food and drinking water, damaging infrastructure and creating road hazards during Australia's hottest and driest year on record. Sources: AFP via phys.org, 'Snipers to cull up to 10,000 camels in drought-stricken Australia' and '5,000 feral camels culled in drought-hit Australia' (Jan 2020); France 24; RTE; CTV News; National Geographic on the feral camel population. DEDUPE: checked %camel%, %australia%, %outback%, %invasive%; the two existing camel rows are both US camel dairies, and the Australian rows cover kangaroo meat, seawater tomatoes and a water licence case. Fresh angle.

Name: One invasive crab can eat 40 clams a day, so Maine chefs started putting it on the menu instead
Copy:
The European green crab has spread through New England waters, and a single crab can eat up to 40 clams in a day and dig six inches down to reach them

Over the past decade the crabs have chewed through eelgrass beds and destabilized shellfish grounds that harvesters had worked for generations

With federal funding the nonprofit Manomet supplied crabs to New England restaurants and ran a Green Crab Week, and chefs built broths, stocks and sauces around them
CTA:
Support shellfish harvesters and local docks

See what is near you on Localize
context: The invasive European green crab has spread through New England waters; a single crab can eat up to 40 clams a day and dig as deep as six inches to reach them, and over the past decade the crabs have chewed through eelgrass beds, destabilized shellfish industries and disrupted the marine food web. Rather than eradication, NOAA funded the Maine and Massachusetts nonprofit Manomet to build demand for a green crab fishery; Manomet worked with chefs, underwrote a Green Crab Week and supplied crabs to New England restaurants. Because the crabs yield little shell meat, chefs use them for broths, stocks and sauces. Sources: Down East Magazine, 'Green Crabs - Maine's Most Delicious Scourge'; Saveur, 'Scientists in Maine Are Fighting Back Against an Invasive Species by Eating It'; CBC coverage of green crab cooking research. LEFT OUT: a roughly $50,000 grant to a Massachusetts company developing a crab broth powder appears in one write-up only and is not in the Copy. DEDUPE: checked %green crab%, %clam%, %invasive%; existing invasive-as-food rows cover nutria, lionfish, iguana, feral hogs and the Illinois copi rename. Fresh angle.
